svg.text: Sickle cell disease: the crisis you can see and the ones you cannot
Common in Ghana, and the dangerous events are not the painful ones
Painful crisis — what actually helps
Analgesia on time, by the clock, not on request
Generous fluids, oral or intravenous
Warmth — cold triggers and prolongs it
Oxygen if saturation is low, and look for infection
Believe the child’s report of pain
Children in crisis are routinely under-treated for pain
Emergencies that are not painful crises
Fever — the spleen has stopped working, so any
fever may be overwhelming infection
Sudden pallor with a big spleen: blood is pooling
in the abdomen and she can die within hours
Weakness on one side, or trouble speaking: stroke
Breathlessness with chest pain and fever
What keeps a Ghanaian child with sickle cell out of hospital
Daily penicillin and full immunisation — because the spleen no longer protects her
Folic acid, a treated net, prompt treatment of every fever, and plenty of fluids
Avoiding cold, dehydration and exhaustion — the three reliable triggers
What the family is often told, wrongly
That the illness is spiritual, or a curse
That one parent is to blame for passing it on
That the child will not live to adulthood
Each belief delays care at the next crisis
The inheritance, explained simply
Both parents carry the trait and are well
Each pregnancy independently: one in four
affected, two in four carriers, one in four not
A previous healthy child changes nothing
